persona.bio: Priya, 33, HR coordinator at a logistics company with about 300 people. She works in Outlook and the company's HR system all day: scheduling interviews, sending offer letters and onboarding emails, answering the same policy questions about leave and benefits, keeping the onboarding checklist in Excel, and writing the monthly HR newsletter. She tried Copilot a few times. She is not sure what the company allows with employee data.

steps.firstStep: I’m an HR coordinator at a logistics company with about 300 employees. Each time someone asks a benefits question, I need a short, friendly reply I can send by email. steps.note: I am an HR coordinator at a logistics company with about 300 employees. I handle onboarding, benefits questions, interviews, employee records and internal communications. I write mostly to employees and new hires, and sometimes to my manager and payroll. My tone is warm, clear and professional, and I keep messages short, usually a few sentences. I point people to the benefits portal or the right team when that is the answer. Never add details I did not give you, like policy numbers, dates, dollar amounts or rules. If something is missing, put it in square brackets so I can fill it in from our approved sources. Always tell me what you assumed.

steps.title: Answering benefits questions, written with AI
steps.read: Claude drafts each benefits answer and waits for your OK. You give it the question and the facts you already have from the benefits portal or payroll, and it writes a clear reply in your voice. That keeps the many daily questions consistent, and you check every answer against your approved sources before it goes out.

material.label: Your benefits question message
items: I am an HR coordinator at a logistics company with about 300 employees. An employee asked me this benefits question: [paste the question without names or personal details]. Here is what I know from our approved sources: [facts from the benefits portal or payroll]. Here is what I still need to confirm: [open points, for example the paid portion with payroll]. Write a short, warm reply in my voice that answers only what I gave you, points them to [where to look in the benefits portal], and says I will follow up on anything unconfirmed. Do not add any details I did not give you. Give back the reply, then list anything you assumed.

steps.title: Your emails, written with AI
steps.read: Claude drafts each email and waits for your OK. You tell it who the email is for and what it needs to say, and it writes a clean draft in your voice. Many of your emails are repeats, so this keeps them steady and leaves you to read and send.

material.label: Your email message
items: I am an HR coordinator at a logistics company with about 300 employees. Write an email to [who it is for, for example a new hire, a candidate or a manager] about [topic]. The key points are: [point one], [point two]. The deadline or next step is [day and time or none]. Keep it short, warm and clear, in my voice, with a plain subject line. Do not add facts, dates or policies I did not give you. Put anything missing in square brackets. Give back the subject line and the email, then list what you assumed.

safeUse: Never type employee names, ID numbers, home addresses, salary details or health information into a chat tool.
Never paste records from your HR system, only the question with the personal details taken out.
Check every benefits answer against the benefits portal or payroll before you send it.
Do not let AI state policy, leave rules or pay details you have not confirmed yourself.
Read every draft before it goes out.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager or IT contact], I would like to use an AI tool to help with my day to day work in HR. I am thinking of drafting replies to benefits questions, writing routine emails and preparing onboarding messages for new hires. Which AI tools are approved at our company, and what may I use them for? I would only use them with personal details removed, and I would read and check everything before it goes out. Could you let me know what is allowed, and whether linking my work email is permitted?

design.today: You answer benefits questions many times a day, mostly by email and at your desk, and also by Teams chat. Your last one was a parental leave question, where you pointed to the benefits portal and said you would confirm the paid portion with payroll.
design.newWay: Because you are not sure your company allows AI for work, the first step is to ask and get a clear answer, and nothing here touches real work until you have it. If the answer is yes, you keep a saved assistant loaded only with your public benefits policy wording, and it drafts a reply from the question you paste in, with no employee names or personal details. You read each draft, check it against the portal, and send it yourself. Answers stay consistent, and anything the policy does not cover is marked for you to confirm with payroll.

steps.goal: Ask your manager or IT whether you may use AI for HR work, and what may be pasted into it, before doing anything else.
Pick the ten benefits questions you get most often and collect the approved policy wording that answers each one.
Get Claude ready on your computer, only if your company says AI is allowed.
Make a project for benefits questions and add the approved policy wording as its reference material.
Set up a saved assistant that drafts benefits replies from the policy wording and flags anything it cannot answer.
Test it with three past questions that have names and personal details removed, and compare each draft with the portal.

design.checkPoint: You read every draft, check it against the benefits portal, and send it yourself, and nothing goes out without you.

design.today: You write a lot of emails, many of them repeats, covering onboarding, policy reminders and interview scheduling.
design.newWay: Your most repeated emails become saved templates in Outlook-style wording, each with clear gaps for names and dates. This works without connecting your work email to anything, since you only copy the finished wording across yourself. For the monthly newsletter and one-off emails, you say what you want out loud or in rough notes, and an AI tool turns it into a draft, but only if your company allows AI. You fill the gaps and read each email before it goes, so the repeats take less effort and still sound like you.

Ask first about your company's AI rules before you use any tool, and give it only the role and start date, never personal details like address or ID numbers.
